newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan scandal seen taking new turn, scaring market.
newsitem.headline: Japan scandal seen taking new turn, scaring market.

text.p: The long-running racketeer payoff scandal gripping Japan's financial industry is likely to take a fresh twist, as speculation grew that top-ranking officials at Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd would be forced to resign.

Top executives at the brokerage are reportedly ready to resign from their posts soon to take responsibility for the brokerage's alleged involvement in the scandal, which already already ensnared Nomura Securities Co Ltd and Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd.

On Friday, prosecutors raided the homes of Yamaichi officials for the third consecutive day in search of evidence of suspected illegal deals with a corporate racketeer at the heart of the high-profile payoff scandal, media reports said.

Meanwhile, in a widely expected move, Yamaichi chairman Tsugio Yukihira offered his resignation as the head of the Japan Securities Dealers' Association (JSDA), an industry body comprising brokerages here.

"I take the situation seriously under which Yamaichi was raided by the authorities. It would not be appropriate to remain chairman, so I would like to resign as soon as possible," Yukihira was quoted as saying by Jiji news agency.
Yamaichi officials remained tight-lipped on the likelihood of Yukihira or president Atsuo Miki resigning from their top post at Yamaichi, one of Japan's "Big Four" brokerages.
The high-profile scandal would continue to be a drag for the fragile Tokyo market by making individual investors shy away from buying shares, brokers here said.

"Such scandals do the worst damage to the stock market by scaring away private investors. The economy is not looking good, which is another reason for them to stay away, and it will take much to repair investor confidence," Noboru Yorita, general manager at Tachibana Securities Co Ltd.

Hit by the worst ever technical glitch on the Tokyo bourse, the market's benchmark Nikkei 225 average plunged to one of its biggest losses this year on Friday. It ended the session down 527.05 points, or nearly three percent, to close at 19,804.38.
It was its first close below 20,000 since July 11 and its sixth-biggest points loss this year.
Fears are also growing in the market that the scandal could widen to ensnare the other "Big Four" brokerages -- Nikko Securities Co Ltd and Daiwa Securities Co Ltd, brokers said.

"There is concern in the market over the next chapter in the scandal...It could turn out that the remaining three brokerages are all involved afterall," Mitsuru Hayashino, Sanyo Securities general manager. "If they are all punished and are all suspended from trading on their own accounts, it would definitely hurt the market," he added.

Despite the gloom over the stock market, Noboru Yorita, general manager at Tachibana Securities Co Ltd, said the worst may be over for the scandal-hit Nomura after long-awaited administrative penalties for its role in a racketeer scandal were announced earlier this week.

Nomura shares marked a new high for this calendar year on Friday, surpassing its previous high, reached before the scandal was first erupted in early March. After hitting a high of 1,740, it ended the day unchanged at 1,680 yen.

Nomura may stand tall as the top Japanese brokerage to brave the nation's "Big Bang" financial reforms, as customers which boycotted Nomura are likely to come back after the punishment period is over.
But unlike Nomura, which is expected to weather stiff penalties, its weaker rival Yamaichi could take a body blow if it suffers the same fate, industry analysts say.
